For existing command-line tools, wrapping them directly with Shell orchestration has the lowest cost; for new tools, natively exposing an MCP interface brings capabilities such as schema validation and tool discovery. The two are not mutually exclusive—in practices like Claude Code, an MCP server is often simply an executor that wraps Shell commands. Another value of MCP lies in ecosystem reuse: the same set of tools can be reused by different Agents and different hosts, reducing tool integration cost from “writing an adapter for each vendor” to “implementing the protocol once.”
ez0pnz:261: MCP (Model Context Protocol) provides CLI Agents with a standardized interface for interacting with external tools. The protocol is based on JSON-RPC 2.0 and adopts a client-server architecture: the Agent acts as a client to connect to various MCP servers, organizing capabilities through the two-layer abstraction of “Resources” and “Tools”—resources are context information fetched passively, while tools are operations triggered actively. This layered design aligns naturally with the CLI design philosophy: the CLI itself is a loop of “enter command → get output → process result,” and MCP turns this loop into a protocolized, structured form.
